courseTitle: The Second British Empire: Commerce, Conquest & Critique (1765–1914)
eyebrow: Key Stage 3 History • Global Empire Enquiry

eras.title: Part 1: Company Tribute, Naval Mastery & Indian De-Industrialisation (1765–1850)
Part 2: Crystal Palace, The 1857 Indian Rebellion & The Crown Raj (1851–1878)
Part 3: The Scramble for Africa, Naval Deterrence & Anti-Colonial Critique (1879–1914)

milestones.title: Mughal Textiles, Calico Tariffs & The 1765 Diwani of Bengal
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did the 1765 Diwani let the Company buy Indian silk without silver?
milestones.imageCaption: Benjamin West, Shah ’Alam Conveying the Grant of the Diwani to Lord Clive, August 1765 (British Library Foster 29): Transferring Bengal tax-collection rights to the East India Company.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: East India Company Rule in Bengal, Textile De-industrialisation, Annexations & The 1857 Indian Rebellion (1765–1858).
milestones.catalyst: Mughal India produced **over a quarter of world textiles**, prompting Britain to shield domestic wool behind the **1700 and 1721 Calico Acts** banning printed Indian cotton imports.
milestones.turningPoint: Under the **August 1765 Treaty of Allahabad**, defeated Emperor **Shah Alam II** granted the **East India Company** the **Diwani**—sovereign power to collect taxes from **20 million people** across Bengal.
milestones.impact: Halted British silver bullion shipments overnight: Company merchants bought Indian silk and muslin using **extracted Bengali peasant taxes**, initiating a vast drain of wealth to London.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Protecting global Company trade and closed **Navigation Act** sea lanes required unchallenged Royal Navy ocean mastery—tested off **Cape Trafalgar in 1805**.

keyTerms.definition: Sovereign right granted in 1765 to collect land taxes across Bengal, allowing the East India Company to buy Indian goods with Indian tax revenues.
The August 1765 settlement transferring fiscal control over Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa from Emperor Shah Alam II to the East India Company.
Protectionist 1700 and 1721 parliamentary laws banning imported printed Indian cottons to shield British textile makers.

milestones.title: Portsmouth Steam Block Mills & Nelson’s Victory at Trafalgar
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Admiral Nelson’s tactics win sea control at Trafalgar in 1805?
milestones.imageCaption: J. M. W. Turner, The Battle of Trafalgar, 21 October 1805 (National Maritime Museum BHC0565): HMS Victory pierces the Franco-Spanish line, securing a century of Royal Navy ocean mastery.
milestones.mapCaption: Admiralty Survey Plan of His Majesty’s Dock Yard at Portsmouth (British Library Maps K.Top.14.42), where Marc Brunel installed steam block mills in 1803.
milestones.catalyst: British **Mercantilism** and the **Navigation Acts** forced colonial sugar and cotton onto British ships, sustained by **10,000 workers** and Marc Brunel’s **1803 steam block mills** at **Portsmouth Royal Dockyard**.
milestones.turningPoint: On **21 October 1805**, **Admiral Lord Nelson** led 27 warships in two attacking columns to shatter 33 French and Spanish battleships off **Cape Trafalgar** without losing a single British ship.
milestones.impact: Secured over a century of **Pax Britannica** across global oceans, enabling Britain to police merchant shipping routes and project imperial gunboat power unhindered.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Protected by Royal Navy sea control, steam-powered **Lancashire cotton mills** flooded Company-ruled India with duty-free factory cloth after **1813**.

keyTerms.definition: Imperial economic policy restricting colonial trade to British ships and ports to accumulate national bullion reserves.
Site of Admiral Lord Nelson’s decisive 21 October 1805 naval triumph over the combined French and Spanish fleets.
Britain’s premier naval industrial complex, pioneering mass production with Marc Brunel’s 1803 steam-powered wooden block mills.

milestones.title: Lancashire Steam Mills & One-Way Colonial Tariff Walls
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Lancashire mills and 70% border taxes ruin Indian weavers?
milestones.imageCaption: Thomas Allom, Power-Loom Weaving in a Lancashire Steam Mill (1835): Protected by steep British import duties against Indian cloth, steam-spun Manchester cotton flooded Indian bazaars.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Reversal of textile trade between industrial Lancashire and colonial Bengal (1813–1850).
milestones.catalyst: High-speed spinning mules and steam powerlooms in **Lancashire** mass-produced millions of yards of cheap cotton yarn, seeking captive overseas colonial markets.
milestones.turningPoint: Parliament imposed **70% to 80% border tariffs** blocking finished Indian textiles from Britain while forcing Company ports in India to admit **British factory cotton** at nominal 2% duties.
milestones.impact: Inverted centuries of global commerce, systematically pricing skilled **Indian spinners and village handloom weavers** out of both European and domestic Indian markets.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Within twenty years, unequal tariffs triggered catastrophic urban collapse across historic Indian weaving capitals such as **Dhaka**.

keyTerms.definition: Northern English heartland of steam-powered cotton mills whose cheap machine cloth flooded colonial Indian markets.
The systematic destruction of India’s artisanal textile manufacturing sector under unequal British tariffs and factory imports.

milestones.title: Devastation of Dhaka’s Weavers & Bentinck’s 1834 Lament
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did collapsing cloth exports affect weaving towns like Dhaka by 1834?
milestones.imageCaption: Processes in the Manufacture of Dacca Muslins (John Forbes Watson, 1866): Recording the intricate Bengali handloom craft devastated by unequal colonial tariffs.
milestones.catalyst: Starved of royal Mughal patronage and undercut by duty-free Manchester cloth, export workshops across **Bengal and Gujarat** shuttered their looms.
milestones.turningPoint: **Dhaka’s** population plunged from 150,000 toward 30,000, prompting Governor-General **Lord William Bentinck** to write in **1834** that **"the bones of the cotton-weavers are bleaching the plains of India"**.
milestones.impact: Transformed India from the world’s premier exporter of luxury finished textiles into an impoverished colonial supplier of **raw cotton, indigo, and jute** for British mills.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Swollen by colonial raw materials and captive markets, mid-Victorian Britain celebrated its industrial zenith at the **May 1851 Great Exhibition**.

keyTerms.definition: Skilled Indian artisans in centres like Dhaka forced into impoverished farm labour when colonial tariffs ruined native cloth exports.
Collapse of native manufacturing industries that reduced colonial economies to exporting raw agricultural commodities.

milestones.title: The Crystal Palace & "Workshop of the World" (1851)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: What did the 1851 Great Exhibition and Koh-i-Noor diamond show?
milestones.imageCaption: The Crystal Palace in Hyde Park for Grand International Exhibition of 1851 (Read & Co., London): Six million visitors viewed British steam machinery alongside colonial treasures.
milestones.catalyst: Backed by Prince Albert and Joseph Paxton’s monumental glass-and-iron **Crystal Palace** in Hyde Park, **Queen Victoria** opened the **Great Exhibition** in May 1851.
milestones.turningPoint: Over **six million visitors** marvelled at 100,000 exhibits—from British steam locomotives and telegraphs to the **Koh-i-Noor diamond** confiscated from child Maharaja Duleep Singh.
milestones.impact: Broadcast Britain’s self-confident claim as the triumphant **"Workshop of the World"**, framing global colonial extraction as providential Victorian progress.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Yet in India, **Lord Dalhousie’s** aggressive annexations of princely kingdoms between **1848 and 1856** were pushing colonial rule toward armed explosion.

keyTerms.definition: Historians who emphasize industrial innovation, global trade integration, and rising British real wages after 1850.
Earlier closed-trade system superseded by mid-Victorian Britain’s dominance as "Workshop of the World".

milestones.title: Lord Dalhousie’s Doctrine of Lapse & Annexation of Awadh
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Dalhousie’s Doctrine of Lapse and seizing Awadh anger Indians?
milestones.imageCaption: James Andrew Broun-Ramsay, 1st Marquess of Dalhousie (Sir John Watson-Gordon, National Portrait Gallery NPG 188): Governor-General whose Doctrine of Lapse and 1856 seizure of Awadh inflamed rebellion.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Dalhousie’s annexations of Satara, Nagpur, Jhansi (1854), and Awadh (1856) across India.
milestones.catalyst: Determined to expand Company tax revenues and territory, Governor-General **Lord Dalhousie** enforced the **Doctrine of Lapse** (1848–1856), overriding Hindu adoption law.
milestones.turningPoint: Whenever a Hindu ruler died without a biological male heir, the Company annexed his state—seizing **Satara, Nagpur, and Jhansi**—before deposing the Nawab of wealthy **Awadh in February 1856**.
milestones.impact: Outraged disinherited royal courts, heavily taxed landowners, and **75,000 Bengal Army sepoys** recruited directly from Awadh’s villages.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Simmering anger over Awadh ignited in **spring 1857** when sepoys were ordered to bite greased cartridges for the new **Pattern 1853 Enfield rifle**.

keyTerms.definition: Lord Dalhousie’s annexation policy seizing any Indian princely state whose ruler died without a biological male heir.
Wealthy northern Indian kingdom annexed in February 1856, alienating thousands of Bengal Army sepoy families.
Indian soldiers recruited and paid to serve in the regiments of the British East India Company.

milestones.title: Enfield Cartridges, The Meerut Uprising & Rani Lakshmibai
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi lead rebel forces until June 1858?
milestones.imageCaption: Rani Lakshmibai Leading Her Troops Against British Forces (19th-Century Indian Gouache, Wellcome Collection): Depicting the warrior queen of Jhansi riding into battle wielding a curved talwar sword.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Northern India — The Mutiny 1857–59 (Cambridge Modern History Atlas), marking Meerut, Delhi, Lucknow, Cawnpore, Jhansi, and Gwalior.
milestones.catalyst: Rumours that **Pattern 1853 Enfield rifle** cartridges had to be bitten open through **cow and pig fat** violated sacred Hindu and Muslim law, sparking fear of forced Christian conversion.
milestones.turningPoint: On **10 May 1857** sepoys mutinied at **Meerut** and proclaimed **Bahadur Shah II** in Delhi, while **Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi** led fierce cavalry resistance until falling in battle at **Gwalior in June 1858**.
milestones.impact: Forged remarkable Hindu-Muslim rebel unity across northern India before British forces suppressed the uprising through ruthless artillery reprisals.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Shocked by the near-loss of India, Westminster moved immediately in **August 1858** to abolish the East India Company forever.

keyTerms.definition: Pattern 1853 musket whose greased paper cartridges—rumoured to contain beef and pork fat—sparked the May 1857 mutinies.
Sovereign Queen of annexed Jhansi who commanded rebel cavalry in 1857–1858 before dying in combat at Gwalior.

milestones.title: The Government of India Act 1858 & Birth of the Crown Raj
milestones.specTag: Corporate Rule Replaced by Crown Viceroy
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did the Government of India Act 1858 change how Britain ruled India?
milestones.imageCaption: Queen Victoria, Proclaimed Empress of India (Kaisar-i-Hind) (1882 portrait by Alexander Bassano): Following the 1858 dissolution of the East India Company, India was governed directly under the Crown Raj.
milestones.catalyst: Fourteen months of fierce war convinced Parliament that a private trading corporation could no longer be trusted to govern **250 million people** across the subcontinent.
milestones.turningPoint: Parliament passed the **Government of India Act (August 1858)** dissolving the East India Company and transferring direct sovereignty to **Queen Victoria** through a royal **Viceroy**.
milestones.impact: Although Victoria’s **November 1858 Proclamation** promised religious non-interference and halted princely annexations, the new **British Raj** entrenched British troop ratios and racial segregation.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Two years later, Britain reinforced its global imperial grip at sea by launching the world’s most powerful ironclad warship: **HMS Warrior (1860)**.

keyTerms.definition: Direct British Crown rule over India (1858–1947) administered by a Viceroy after the abolition of the East India Company.
Authoritarian imperial ideology claiming British officials ruled colonized peoples as stern, superior guardians.

milestones.title: HMS Warrior & The Ironclad Warship Revolution
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did HMS Warrior make wooden battleships outdated in 1860?
milestones.imageCaption: Archival Broadside Photograph of Ironclad Warship HMS Warrior (c. 1861–1867, Royal Navy): Built with 4.5-inch wrought-iron armour backed by eighteen inches of solid teak.
milestones.catalyst: French naval experiments with armoured hulls threatened to erode the sailing-fleet dominance Britain had enjoyed since Nelson’s triumph at Trafalgar.
milestones.turningPoint: In **1860** Britain launched **HMS Warrior**, sheathing an iron hull in **4.5-inch wrought-iron armour** backed by **18 inches of teak**, propelled by twin steam engines and rifled guns.
milestones.impact: Bouncing enemy shells off its sides in live trials, *Warrior* rendered **every wooden battleship on Earth obsolete overnight** and locked in British maritime technological supremacy.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Industrial engineering also transformed colonial interiors through **railways and submarine cables**, yet collided fatally with **1876–1878 famine policy** in India.

keyTerms.definition: Britain’s revolutionary 1860 steam-powered, iron-armoured warship that made wooden sailing battleships obsolete.
Historic home berth and industrial maintenance hub for Britain’s ironclad and steam battle fleets.

milestones.title: Imperial Railways, Telegraphs & The 1876–1878 Great Famine
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did ten million Indians starve while grain was shipped to Britain?
milestones.imageCaption: The Famine in India — Distribution of Relief to the Sufferers at Bellary, Madras Presidency (1877): Viceroy Lord Lytton refused to halt grain exports while millions perished.
milestones.catalyst: Colonial engineers built **25,000 miles of Indian railways** and laid submarine telegraph cables (`SS Great Eastern`, 1866) designed to rush **cash crops** to ports and troops to unrest.
milestones.turningPoint: When monsoon rains failed across southern India (**1876–1878**), **Viceroy Lord Lytton** enforced rigid **laissez-faire** market dogma, refusing to cap grain prices or halt **record wheat exports** to Britain.
milestones.impact: Starving peasants were forced into punitive hard-labour camps on minimal rations as **millions perished** across late-Victorian famines, exposing the lethal cost of colonial economic policy.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Even as famine devastated India, European industrial powers turned in **1879–1885** to partitioning the **African continent**.

keyTerms.definition: Historians who emphasize de-industrialisation, coercive extraction, and preventable late-Victorian famines under imperial rule.
Critique showing colonial railways and taxes exported Indian grain and wealth to Britain without fair return.

milestones.title: Zulu Resistance, The Berlin Conference & Effective Occupation
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did fourteen Western nations meet in Berlin in 1884 with no Africans?
milestones.imageCaption: Satirical Cartoon on the Berlin Conference: King Leopold II Carving the "Congo" Above a Map of "Afrique" (Le Frondeur, 20 December 1884).
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: The Scramble for Africa, Imperial Partition & African Resistance (1879–1914)—marking Zululand, Berlin’s geometric borders, Suez-to-Cape, and the Congo.
milestones.catalyst: After **King Cetshwayo’s** Zulu regiments stunned British invaders at **Isandlwana (1879)** before being overwhelmed, rival European powers raced for African rubber, copper, palm oil, and diamonds.
milestones.turningPoint: Hosted by **Otto von Bismarck** in **1884–1885**, **fourteen Western powers** met in Berlin with **zero African leaders invited**, decreeing **"Effective Occupation"** as the rule for claiming territory.
milestones.impact: Forced empires to march garrisons inland to plant flags, slicing ancient African kingdoms with geometric borders and colonising **90% of Africa by 1914**.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Escalating imperial rivalry with France, Russia, and Germany pushed Westminster in **March 1889** to lock naval supremacy into statute law.

keyTerms.definition: Summit of fourteen Western powers in Berlin establishing rules for partitioning Africa with zero African delegates present.
Berlin Conference rule requiring physical troops, forts, and administration inland to validate European territorial claims.
Rapid European invasion and partition of roughly 90% of the African continent between 1881 and 1914.

milestones.title: The Naval Defence Act 1889 & The Two-Power Standard
milestones.enquiryQuestion: What did the 1889 Two-Power Standard require from the Royal Navy?
milestones.imageCaption: Steam Tactics of the Reserve Squadron — HMS Thunderer, HMS Warspite, and HMS Galatea (Illustrated London News, July 1897): Expanded under the £21.5 million Naval Defence Act of 1889.
milestones.mapCaption: Walter Crane, Imperial Federation Map of the World Showing the Extent of the British Empire in 1886 (The Graphic, 24 July 1886).
milestones.catalyst: Rapid naval expansion by **France, Russia, and newly unified Germany** threatened the scattered sea lanes binding Britain’s global empire together.
milestones.turningPoint: In **March 1889**, Parliament passed the **£21.5 million Naval Defence Act**, legally establishing the **Two-Power Standard**: the Royal Navy had to match the **next two strongest fleets combined**.
milestones.impact: Triggered a massive battleship construction boom at **Portsmouth** and royal dockyards, cementing maritime deterrence across every ocean.
milestones.bridgeToNext: While armoured fleets guarded the seas, **quinine medicine** and the **Maxim machine gun** unleashed devastating battlefield asymmetry inland at **Omdurman (1898)**.

keyTerms.definition: Statutory 1889 policy requiring the Royal Navy to maintain battleship strength equal to the next two largest foreign navies combined.
Private syndicate—such as Cecil Rhodes’s British South Africa Company (1889)—granted royal military powers overseas.

milestones.title: Quinine, Hiram Maxim’s Machine Gun & The Battle of Omdurman
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did quinine medicine and Maxim guns enable conquest in Africa?
milestones.imageCaption: Omdurman — The First Battle, 2 September 1898 (A. Sutherland chromolithograph, Wellcome Collection V0041182): Marking General Kitchener’s belt-fed Maxim machine-gun batteries.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Britain’s Suez-to-Cape imperial axis, Omdurman in Sudan (1898), and Matabeleland.
milestones.catalyst: Anti-malarial **quinine** extracted from cinchona bark enabled European columns to survive equatorial fevers, while **Hiram Maxim’s** automatic gun fired **600 rounds per minute**.
milestones.turningPoint: On **2 September 1898** at **Omdurman** in Sudan, General Kitchener’s Maxim batteries and artillery slaughtered **over 10,000 Mahdist fighters** for the loss of fewer than fifty Anglo-Egyptian troops.
milestones.impact: Demonstrated the lethal technological gulf of late-Victorian conquest as chartered companies like **Cecil Rhodes’s** seized gold and diamond lands across southern Africa.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Five months after Omdurman, poet **Rudyard Kipling** published **"The White Man’s Burden"** to cloak violent conquest in moral language—challenged by Congo atrocity investigations.

keyTerms.definition: World’s first recoil-operated automatic machine gun (600 rounds per minute), giving colonial armies overwhelming firepower.
Commercial syndicate wielding private armies—like Rhodes’s Maxim-armed columns in Matabeleland—to seize mineral wealth.

milestones.title: "The White Man’s Burden", Rubber Plunder & E. D. Morel’s Expose
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did King Leopold II’s rubber quotas cause terror across the Congo?
milestones.imageCaption: Rudyard Kipling (Elliott & Fry, June 1895): Author of February 1899’s "The White Man’s Burden", whose "civilising mission" myth was shattered by E. D. Morel’s Congo rubber expose.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: King Leopold II’s Congo Free State rubber regime at the heart of partitioned Africa.
milestones.catalyst: In **February 1899**, **Rudyard Kipling** published *"The White Man’s Burden"*, dehumanising colonised peoples as *"half-devil and half-child"* to portray conquest as selfless Christian duty.
milestones.turningPoint: Investigative journalist **E. D. Morel** exposed the reality behind imperial rhetoric in **King Leopold II’s Congo Free State**: hostage-taking, burned villages, and **severed hands** for missed rubber quotas.
milestones.impact: With **millions of Congolese** perishing before international outrage forced Leopold to surrender personal rule in **1908**, Morel shattered the moral facade of European imperialism.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Simultaneously in Westminster and Bombay, economist **Dadabhai Naoroji** marshalled official British tax ledgers to indict imperial rule in India.

keyTerms.definition: Condescending racial ideology claiming European empires acted as benevolent "father figures" civilising colonised societies.
Historical approach centring the lived experiences, suffering, and agency of colonised peoples rather than imperial elites.

milestones.title: Dadabhai Naoroji’s "Drain of Wealth" & The Historiographical Verdict
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How do Niall Ferguson and Shashi Tharoor disagree over the Empire?
milestones.imageCaption: Dadabhai Naoroji Upon Election as MP for Finsbury Central (The Strand Magazine, December 1892): Britain’s first Indian MP published Poverty and Un-British Rule in India in 1901.
milestones.catalyst: Elected in **1892** as Westminster’s **first Indian MP**, economist **Dadabhai Naoroji** audited colonial budgets from 1867 onward to measure the true financial impact of the Raj.
milestones.turningPoint: In *Poverty and Un-British Rule in India* (**1901**), Naoroji proved his **"Drain of Wealth"** theory: Britain siphoned millions in Indian taxes annually to pay London pensions and imperial wars without return.
milestones.impact: Naoroji’s critique anchors today’s fierce debate between **Niall Ferguson** (highlighting common law, trade, and railways) and **Shashi Tharoor** (indicting de-industrialisation, racism, and famine).
milestones.bridgeToNext: Completes the chronological arc of the Second British Empire from the 1765 Bengal Diwani to anti-colonial critique and modern historical debate.

keyTerms.definition: Dadabhai Naoroji’s economic proof that Britain systematically extracted vast tax revenues and resources from India without fair return.
The study of how historians—such as Niall Ferguson and Shashi Tharoor—construct competing interpretations of the past.
Combining contrasting historical evidence and rival interpretations into a balanced, substantiated overall judgement.
